topic: Ordewell: turning one product goal into an ordered plan of coding-agent tasks
notes: Researched 2026-09-29 by run 52f265ac-ea30-422c-b0fc-632ee3858a78 (Researcher, BLO-3423). A concurrent unfiltered Researcher run (7b898199-a28b-4a1f-a8c7-eecf4e9dbe7a) was alive on the same heartbeat; no brief existed for this slug at write time. curl/urllib + official APIs only — no browser tools used.
what_it_is: Ordewell (ordewell.ai, github.com/ordewell/ordewell) is an Apache-2.0, TypeScript task orchestrator for coding agents, published on npm as `ordewell` and `@ordewell/cli`. One plain-prose goal becomes an editable, dependency-ordered plan; every task names its own runner (Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode), model, thinking effort and mode; tasks run in parallel in separate git worktrees, and each task counts as done only when its unique completion marker appears in that runner's output. Surfaces: CLI, terminal UI (TUI, needs tmux), VS Code / Open VSX extension, and a local HTTP+WebSocket API on 127.0.0.1:3742 that the other three are clients of.

competitors.title: Ordewell — Documentation (primary source)
key_points: Install: `npm install -g ordewell` (or `npx ordewell`); VS Code extension `code --install-extension ordewell.ordewell` bundles its own core and needs nothing from npm.
Requirements: Node.js 20+, at least one of Claude Code / Codex / OpenCode, tmux for the TUI on every platform (each task's live terminal is tmux-backed), git for isolation.

No API key required: a coding agent you already pay for can be the planner, launched read-only (`--permission-mode plan`, `sandbox: read-only`, `agent: plan`). With a key, 25 providers are recognised from their own *_API_KEY vars; `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL` covers local/OpenAI-compatible servers.
Headless loop is four commands: `ordewell plan --goal "..."` → edit → `ordewell run` → `ordewell handoff review|merge|discard|cleanup`.

Editing the plan is runner → model → effort → mode, in that order, because each choice constrains the next; setting a runner re-picks model/effort/mode from that runner's real catalog so an unstartable assignment is never saved.
No surface reorders tasks — deliberately: the orchestrator fans out every task whose dependencies are met, so display order was never the schedule. Dependencies are the only lever.

Verdict rule: completion marker decides, exit code is supporting evidence, model opinion is never consulted. `/complete` and `/uncomplete` override by hand; `/verify` appends a final suite-running task judged by exit code.

Isolation: each AI task runs in its own worktree on its own branch; passing work is `git merge --no-ff`'d into one per-run integration branch lowest plan order first; dependents start only once the work is actually on that branch. Nothing reaches the checked-out branch until handoff.

Merge conflicts get up to `conflictRepairAttempts` (default 2, 0 disables) self-repair attempts in the kept worktree; a repair counts only if git agrees — otherwise the task waits with the conflicting files named.

Multi-repo: opening a folder of repositories gives each task a worktree of every repo at its relative path, all on one branch name, so relative paths keep working; a task lands in all repos it changed or none.
Runners are external CLIs, not internal APIs; anything else is a plugin manifest (JSON with {{variable}} / {{if}} templating) installed via `ordewell plugins install github:user/repo`.
Every slash command has an `ordewell` subcommand of the same name, held by a parity test, so headless automation reaches everything a human can.

competitors.title: github.com/ordewell/ordewell — repository and README
key_points: Feature list: editable plan, right model per task, isolated execution, verdicts from evidence, a planner that cannot write, no extra API key, four surfaces sharing one core.

Workflow is 5 steps: Plan, Execute (fresh session per task in its own worktree, 3 concurrent by default), Verify (marker in runner output), Land (merge into integration branch in plan order), Hand off (review diff, merge/discard/cleanup).
Design decisions are public as 17 ADRs under docs/adr/, plus CONTEXT.md defining project vocabulary — unusually auditable for a 2-month-old project.
Skills /grilling, /to-spec and /improve-codebase-architecture, plus TDD task augmentation, are adapted from Matt Pocock's skills repo (MIT).
Ordewell name and logos are excluded from the Apache-2.0 grant via NOTICE.

competitors.title: Ordewell — Plan-first orchestration vs parallel worktree sessions
key_points: Positions the category as two shapes: fan-out parallel worktree sessions vs plan-first orchestration. Both legitimate; they fail in different places.

Core argument: plan-first moves decomposition out of an agent's context and into a typed artifact. 'A bad plan you can see and edit costs a minute. A bad plan that already executed costs an afternoon.'
Review of intent vs review of result — the intent review is cheaper because nothing has been written yet.

Self-declared honest limits: the completion marker proves the session finished and emitted evidence, not that the code compiles or the change is right; the planner is an LLM and writes bad plans sometimes; ordered execution means fewer concurrent sessions than a fan-out board; the TUI needs tmux everywhere.
States parallelism as 'three by default, five at most' — contradicts the docs config table and homepage (see doc_discrepancies).

Disclosure discipline worth noting: the author says plainly he builds the plan-first tool, describes the alternative as a class rather than naming products he has not audited, and tells readers to pick the other shape when it fits.

competitors.title: Ordewell — How to tell when a coding agent has actually finished
key_points: Names the three signals that fail: the terminal went quiet, the process exited 0, and the agent said it was done (the dangerous one, because it is confident).
The fix is evidence: a per-task unique token, requested on the prompt's final line, watched for in the runner's own output.

Non-obvious engineering: a naive `output.includes(token)` fails, because a PTY stream is a rendering protocol — ANSI/OSC escapes, box-drawing gutters, cursor moves and repaints can split or overwrite the token. So there are two scans: a chronological flatten (strip escapes, box-drawing range, whitespace) and a screen replay of cursor/erase sequences; if either sees the token, the task passed.
Attribution rule stated explicitly: one token per task, not per plan or run — a shared token means task six passes on task two's evidence.
The page frames the method as a convention adoptable in any harness, not just a product feature.

competitors.title: Ordewell — How big should a task be in an agent plan
key_points: The unit of size is one session: task sizing is a context decision. Add more and the session starts compacting, so the second half of the work happens without the first half in view.

Practical test: could an engineer who has never seen the repo finish this from the prompt plus the files it names? If the prompt says 'then the same thing at the other eight call sites', it is too big.
Cut vertically, not by layer — a layer plan (types → serializer → CLI wiring → tests) is fully serialized, nothing is demoable alone, and the reviewable diff is the sum of sessions.
Small has a floor: if two adjacent tasks would touch the same function for the same reason, they are one task (each extra task pays a session and re-does research nobody wrote down).
Put the enabling refactor first, as its own task — its crisp bar is that the suite stays green, and dependent slices then declare it as a dependency.
Exception for codebase-wide refactors: sequence expand → migrate → contract, so the repository works at every boundary and one failed batch costs one batch.

competitors.title: Ordewell — Do you need a PRD before a coding agent starts?
key_points: Splits two conflated documents: a plan answers 'what do I run next' and is written for the scheduler; a PRD answers 'why is this correct' and is written for the argument you will have with yourself in three days.
A PRD pays for itself when work will be revised, when tasks must trace back to intent (copy the user-story text into tasks rather than paraphrasing), and when more than one person must agree.

It is busywork when the goal is already fully specified, and when the unknowns are in the code rather than in your head — writing a spec on top of a repository you have not read specifies the wrong system beautifully.

The middle path is questions before the plan: read → ask → plan. The planner is told to ask only when the goal is vague or the answer would materially change the outcome, and that interrogating a user who already said what they want is its own failure mode.
When a PRD does exist it is saved to .scratch/<slug>/PRD.md and the revision pass re-reads it, so a plan can be checked against the whole feature instead of the last few messages.

competitors.title: Ordewell — One plan, several models: choosing an executor per task
key_points: Diagnoses where model choice normally lives, none of it reviewable: inside the prompt text, inside a coordinator model's head, or in a relaunch where you pay the context-explanation cost twice.
A task carries four reviewable fields plus dependencies: runner, model, thinking effort, mode.
Model ids are validated against the task's runner's real catalog, not a global list — `ordewell task-model 4` with no value prints the discovered catalog with the current pick starred.
Effort levels do not survive every model change: some models expose five levels, some none, so switching can drop the effort you set.

competitors.title: tomrochette.com — Ordewell research note (independent, agent-curated)
key_points: Independent 2026-09-27 review, status 'finished', ~974 words. Calls the plan-as-typed-artifact plus marker-not-model verdict 'the design worth stealing'.

Measured at 2026-09-27: 162 stars, 13 forks, 42 open issues (most filed as a single-day roadmap on 2026-09-26), created 2026-07-31, latest release v0.5.4 (2026-09-26), v0.5.x opened 2026-09-25 with five releases in two days after v0.4.23, ~3,500 npm downloads/month across both package names.

Records the launch thread's transparency problem as an adoption consideration: commenters observed everything about the project including the author's replies was AI-written; the maintainer confirmed heavy AI use for code and docs while standing behind the design.
Notes the standing structural objection to meta-frameworks — any advance gets absorbed into Claude and Codex within months, and a planner-plus-runners surface is exactly the kind absorption targets.
Flags churn risk: ADR-0002 records saved sessions being wiped without migration on that rewrite.
States the planner's shell control is a denylist classifier over a real shell, not a sandbox, with ADR-0011 tracking the gap.

competitors.title: Show HN: Ordewell – turn one goal into an ordered plan of coding-agent tasks (HN thread)
key_points: 56 points, 35 comments as fetched 2026-09-29 (launched 2026-09-15); the independent review logged 50 points / 30 comments on 2026-09-27.

The most substantive thread is about weak models: a commenter wanted a deterministic planner for deepseek-class runners, arguing AGENTS.md is not enough; the author replied that AGENTS.md is prose the model re-interprets every session, whereas here the plan is parsed and enforced as structured data with declared dependencies, so the per-step job is smaller and the plan is not up for renegotiation.
Author's own framing of the intended win: a frontier model builds the plan once, then it is fixed and the executing model cannot reinterpret it — which helps a small model that only has to execute.
Author conceded he has not benchmarked against deepseek-class runners and has not quantified on any benchmark, citing cost and the difficulty of testing large undefined tasks.

A practitioner countered that the details matter: too rigid a plan makes agents thrash on self-manufactured work, too little makes them get lost, and the integration strategy is partly forced by cost (e.g. subscription discounts via a vendor TUI).

Absorption objection on the thread: 'any advance just gets rolled into Claude and Codex a few months later'; the author's answer is model/provider agnosticism so you are not locked to one vendor's two or three models.

Transparency exchange: commenter observed everything including author replies was AI-written; maintainer confirmed heavy AI use for docs and code, and separately denied using an LLM for the replies themselves. Another commenter called AI-generated replies disrespectful. Treat discourse hygiene as part of the adoption decision.

competitors.title: github/spec-kit — the spec-first alternative
key_points: Adjacent, not the same shape: Spec Kit produces a specification, technical plan and tasks that guide a single agent through implementation; Ordewell produces a task graph that a scheduler executes across multiple agents, models and worktrees.
139,316 stars / 12,481 forks, MIT, created 2025-08-21, last pushed 2026-09-28 (fetched 2026-09-29) — the gravity in the 'structure before code' space sits here, not with the orchestrators.
Three independent entry points rather than three mandatory phases: spec-driven development, bug fixing, idea assessment. Requires Python 3.11+ and uv; installs via `uv tool install specify-cli`.
Workflow is constitution once per project, then specify → plan → tasks → implement → converge per feature, invoked as /speckit-* agent skills inside any supported coding agent.

competitors.title: eyaltoledano/claude-task-master (Taskmaster) — task-management comparison
key_points: Closest conceptual competitor: an AI-powered task-management system dropped into Cursor, Windsurf, Roo, Lovable and others, with task dependencies, tags/workstreams, a research command and a loop command.
28,107 stars / 2,616 forks, license NOASSERTION (MIT with a Commons Clause), 54,336 npm downloads in the last month on `task-master-ai`.
Maintenance signal: repo created 2025-03-04 but last pushed 2026-04-28 — roughly five months stale as of 2026-09-29, which is the strongest concrete caution in this comparison set.
Key architectural difference to draw: Taskmaster manages tasks inside the IDE/chat you already use; Ordewell owns execution too — per-task runner, model, worktree, integration branch and verdict.

competitors.title: BloopAI/vibe-kanban — the kanban-board shape
key_points: 28,212 stars / 3,027 forks, Apache-2.0, but only 10 commits on the default branch since 2026-06-01 and a latest commit dated 2026-09-19; Bloop announced its shutdown in April 2026 and the project is now community-run.
Models tasks rather than sessions, which is the right abstraction when losing track of tasks is the failure you feel.

Comparison axis for the article: a board answers 'what is the state of my fleet'; a plan answers 'what is the order of this work and who runs which step'. Ordewell deliberately refuses to reorder tasks for this reason.

competitors.title: crystl.dev — Best AI Agent Orchestration Tools for Coding (2026 Comparison)
key_points: Useful taxonomy: separate pipeline orchestration (LangGraph, CrewAI, n8n, Airflow — backend problems) from local coding-agent orchestration (a workspace problem), and judge tools on four axes: isolation, visibility, unblocking, review-and-merge.

Pricing and status verified 17 August 2026: Conductor (macOS, worktree, free tier / Pro $50/mo / Teams $60 per user); Vibe Kanban (free, Apache-2.0, unmaintained); crystl (macOS, free tier / Guild $170/yr); Claude Squad (free, AGPL-3.0, Go + tmux); Cursor cloud agents (from $20/mo); Sculptor (free, MIT); Claude Code agent teams (included).
Vendor-disclosed page (crystl is the publisher's own tool) — treat the competitor prices as second-hand and re-check vendor pages before publishing numbers.

Argues that isolation is table stakes (every serious tool uses a git worktree, container or cloud VM) and that the differentiator is unblocking: an idle agent waiting on approval looks identical to a finished one.

competitors.title: agentsroom.dev — The Best Tools to Run Multiple Coding Agents in 2026
key_points: Isolation taxonomy worth reusing: git worktrees (cheap, fast, but a runaway install still touches the real machine), Docker containers (a mistake stays in the sandbox, heavier), cloud VMs (someone else's machine, you wait and pay).
Same vendor-tool caveat as crystl — agentsroom markets its own product in the same list; use it for the taxonomy, not for the verdicts.
Notes Claude Squad is 'actively maintained' while Vibe Kanban is community-run after the Bloop shutdown, and that Conductor is macOS/Apple-Silicon only with no multi-project management.

competitors.title: laxaar.com — Agent Planning: ReAct vs Plan-and-Execute Tradeoffs
key_points: Supplies the theory under the product: ReAct interleaves thought/action/observation one step at a time; plan-and-execute generates a full plan up front and then runs each step with only the context that step needs.

Cost claim: a 10-step ReAct task on Claude Sonnet can cost 3-5x more than the equivalent plan-and-execute run, because each ReAct step re-processes the full accumulated context. Crossover point in the author's experience is around four to five steps; below that the planner's latency tax (~3s) makes ReAct faster.

Failure modes to contrast: ReAct's reasoning loop can convince itself at step seven that the task needs a different approach and start over; it also degrades as context grows because signal-to-noise falls. Plan-and-execute handles discovery poorly — a rigid upfront plan can be irrelevant by step three.
Plan-and-execute is the only one of the two that opens up step-level parallelism, which is exactly the property Ordewell's dependency graph exploits.
Debuggability: plan-and-execute step traces are discrete spans that Langfuse/Arize Phoenix/Helicone surface cleanly; a ReAct trace is one long span with nested tool calls.
Mitigations named: replanning triggers, hierarchical planning, bounded ReAct with a hard step budget.

competitors.title: OrchBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Plans in Isolation via Deterministic Simulation (arXiv 2607.25656)
key_points: Peer-adjacent evidence that orchestration-plan quality is separable from worker capability: OrchBench builds DAGs encoding task dependencies from real-world tasks with controlled size and parallelism, then scores a planner's assignments with a deterministic simulator that never invokes worker agents.
Simulated scores correlate strongly with quality scores from real Claude Code executions (Pearson r = 0.816) at 1.3% of the tokens and 10.3% of the wall-clock time.

Two findings directly relevant to a plan-first how-to: preserving task-critical information matters more than simply adding more agents, and the benefits of parallelism diminish as coordination failures accumulate.
Caveat to state in the article: this is a 2026 arXiv preprint (submitted 28 July 2026, cs.AI, 8 authors) and is not peer-reviewed; use it for the direction of the result, not as a settled number.

stats.fact: Vendor-documented defaults: ORDEWELL_MAX_PARALLEL = 3, ORDEWELL_WORKTREE_ISOLATION = true, ORDEWELL_CONFLICT_REPAIR_ATTEMPTS = 2, planner model default deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash, 25 recognised providers, local API on 127.0.0.1:3742.

The planner is a cheap model by design: the maintainer's design note says decomposition is a bounded reading-and-reasoning task that does not need the strongest coding model, while code generation should get the strongest model only for that change — and lists the default planner as deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash via OpenRouter or a Gemini Flash-class model.

Verdict mechanism is marker-based, not model-based: the completion marker decides, exit code is kept as evidence, and the model is never consulted. The implementation flattens ANSI/OSC escapes, box-drawing gutters and whitespace, then re-replays cursor/erase sequences to reconstruct the visible screen, scanning both views.
stats.source: ordewell.ai/agent-completion (vendor self-report, implementation detail shown in code)

stats.fact: ADR-0008 documents the planner's exploration envelope as three tiers — auto (read-only inspection runs unprompted), ask (one approval, remembered per session scope), refuse (writes, privilege escalation, output redirection, piping into an interpreter, inline -c/-e code: never runs, never prompts) — plus path confinement, ~-expansion before resolution, one in-flight ask per scope, and 'absent is denial' including a five-minute timeout.

The same ADR records concrete pre-fix bugs worth citing as the cost of a denylist design: `ls docs/removed` tripped the `rm` rule and `git show HEAD:src/kill.ts` tripped `kill` (substring matching), splitting on a bare /[|;&]/ made `rg "error|warn" src` ask for approval scoped to a nonsense binary, and an unexpanded `~` let an auto-tier `cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa` read the real file because path.resolve treated it as inside the workspace.
The project itself states the planner's shell control is a denylist over a real shell rather than an OS-level sandbox, with ADR-0011 tracking that gap; an independent reviewer repeats the caution.
stats.source: ADR-0008 preamble, ADR-0011 (title: sandboxing the planner's shell), tomrochette.com

stats.fact: Worktree layout is documented and deterministic: worktrees at .ordewell/worktrees/<run-id>/<order>-<slug>, task branches ordewell/<run-id>/<order>-<slug>, integration branch ordewell/<run-id>/integration, merges via git merge --no-ff lowest plan order first, and the integration branch gets its own worktree because the user's checkout is off limits.
The product has no hosted service, no paid tier, and does not proxy model calls; an independent reviewer role is explicitly listed as open work rather than a claimed feature.

Plan-and-execute can cost roughly 3-5x less than ReAct on a 10-step task on Claude Sonnet (each ReAct step re-processes the full accumulated context), with the crossover around four to five steps once the planner's ~3s latency tax is counted.

angles: The plan is a typed artifact, not a train of thought. The whole article can hang on this one idea: decomposition normally lives in a prompt and an agent's context, where it cannot be edited and can only be undone; Ordewell writes it as JSON you rewrite before a token is spent. Frame the cost of being wrong — a minute for an editable plan versus an afternoon for one that already executed.

Stop asking the model whether it finished. Ordewell's verdict rule is a unique per-task marker scanned in the runner's output, with exit codes kept only as evidence and the model never consulted. The honest limits matter for credibility: a marker proves the session ended and emitted its evidence, not that the code compiles.

Why the marker scan is harder than it looks. A PTY stream is a rendering protocol, not a document — ANSI/OSC escapes, box-drawing gutters, soft wraps and full-screen repaints can split or overwrite the token, which is why a naive output.includes() misses it and the tool needs both a chronological flatten and a screen replay. This is the single most concrete, least-covered implementation detail available for the article.

One goal, four assignments per task. Runner, model, thinking effort and mode are chosen per task, validated against that runner's real catalog, and visible before execution. The argument to make is about where the decision normally lives: in a prompt sentence, in a coordinator's head, or in a relaunch where you pay the explanation cost twice.

The planner cannot write, and the refusal is not promptable. ADR-0008's auto/ask/refuse tiers, path confinement and absent-is-denial rule give the article a defensible section on read-only planning — and the ADR's own bug list (ls docs/removed tripping rm, an unexpanded ~ reading ~/.ssh/id_rsa) is unusually honest evidence for why prompt-level 'do not modify files' is not a sandbox.

Task sizing is the real skill, not tool selection. One session per task, cut vertically not by layer, put the enabling refactor first, expand-then-contract for codebase-wide changes, and the floor rule that two adjacent tasks touching the same function are one task. A step-by-step method readers can apply to their own backlog even without installing anything.

Plan-first versus fan-out is a fork in the road, not a ranking. Fan-out wins for independent work and for watching and steering; plan-first wins for ordered work, for leaving the room, and for mixed models per task. Ordewell's own comparison page concedes fan-out is what the market rewards — use that concession to keep the article fair.

The adoption-verdict section writes itself honestly: two months old, 179 stars, v0.5.5 with five releases in two days, ADR-0002 documenting saved sessions wiped without migration, a denylist classified over a real shell rather than an OS sandbox, and a launch thread where the maintainer confirmed heavy AI use across code and docs. A young tool whose design is worth stealing today.
